cases.title: Bumbuna hydroelectric dam: 5,033 people compensated, two villages left out
cases.place: Bumbuna, Kalanthuba chiefdom, Tonkolili District, Sierra Leone
cases.point: Bumbuna town, below the dam on the Seli River (OpenStreetMap). The Bank's documents give no coordinates for the 38 villages that lost land to the reservoir.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Grants IDA-H1700 and IDA-H6250 for the Bumbuna Hydroelectric Environmental and Social Management Project (P086801). An IDA grant of US$12.5 million was approved on 16 June 2005 alongside a partial risk guarantee for the dam; the grant was later raised to US$22.0 million. The original commitment of SDR 8.30 million became SDR 13.21 million disbursed. Effectiveness was 19 December 2006 against an original date of 26 October 2005, and closing was 30 June 2013 against an original date of 31 August 2009. The project was restructured seven times and renamed in 2011, when the guarantee was cancelled and US$9.5 million moved into the environmental and social work. Outcomes were rated Moderately Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 July 2014).

lenders.name: African Development Bank
lenders.role: US$3.8 million in the project's original and revised financing plan. Italy (US$19.9 million), OPEC (US$8.4 million) and the Netherlands (US$0.3 million) were in the original plan and nil in the revised plan (World Bank completion report, Annex 1).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement, safety of dams, natural habitats, forests and cultural property. An exception to the Bank's resettlement policy was granted so that IDA grant money could pay 'legacy' compensation for property and farmland lost when the transmission line foundations were first built in the 1990s. A special account was set up for transmission line compensation, to be used once a legal framework existed.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report says the environmental assessments and resettlement action plans entailed 'resettlement and compensation covering 38 villages, 599 households, and 5,033 PAPs', emergency food aid over two years, land-for-land exchange for 41 households (186 people) in five villages covering 179.3 hectares, and cash compensation to 171 farmers with 117 hectares of partly or fully flooded farmland. The report says 41 houses in five villages were resettled for US$286,370. For the 161 kV transmission line, the 2005 plan found 367 households inside the right of way; under revised rules in 2009 about 910 households and 1,565 people were found inside the built-up parts of the right of way, and 70 to 80 per cent of them chose to move elsewhere. A resurvey in 2011 found about 100 new affected people, that 142 of the 507 boundary markers placed in 2007 had gone missing after the reservoir filled, and that more than 500 'shoreline farmers' were using the land in the dry season. A 2024 field study at Addis Ababa's distance from the Bank's files reaches a different conclusion about two of the villages: Katherine Stevick's master's thesis for Colorado State University, based on interviews and participatory mapping in Kalanthuba chiefdom in 2023, says Kamathor lost more than half its historic landholdings and Kadala all of its, that there are detailed reports at the project camp of how compensation was paid in Kalanthuba 'with Kadal and Kamathor mistakenly omitted', and that Kadala was not compensated because it had not been predicted to lose farmland to the flooded area.
cases.ecosystem: The reservoir and a buffer zone took land for the Bumbuna Conservation Area, chartered by Sierra Leone's parliament in 2008 and covering 3,532 hectares entirely inside Kalanthuba chiefdom, created after the Bank's environmental study showed the dam would harm a rare population of West African chimpanzees. A larger offset was later added by upgrading the Loma Mountains forest reserve to a national park. The 2024 thesis says it found no report of any process to compensate for land taken for the conservation area, and that staff of the Bumbuna Watershed Management Authority knew of none.
cases.killed_note: Two boys from Bumbuna Town died during one of the large water releases from the dam in January 2009, which the Bank's completion report calls an accidental death and says prompted clearer emergency warning procedures.
cases.displaced_label: people compensated or resettled around the dam and reservoir (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 8,862 for this project. The World Bank's completion report says resettlement and compensation covered 38 villages, 599 households and 5,033 project-affected persons by December 2008, and that 41 households (186 people) in five villages were physically moved and given replacement land. For the transmission line it gives about 910 households and 1,565 people inside the built-up right of way in 2009. The documents do not explain the difference from ICIJ's figure, and no document found gives a single total of people relocated.
cases.outcome: The Bank says the three resettlement targets were fully met and that livelihoods were restored to pre-project levels 'barring a few cases where the PAPs are not contactable'. The same report says compensation remained to be paid on legacy claims and that 95 people could not be found because they had left the area, and that at closing in June 2013 'conformance to the provisions of the Bank's environmental and social safeguards policies was incomplete', with payment of compensation to the few remaining affected people among the items the Bank would keep supervising after the project ended. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 2 December 2015 records the same unfinished items and says the completion report gives little or no information on four of the six safeguard policies the project triggered. The borrower and implementing agencies did not comment on the completion report despite multiple reminders. The 2024 thesis says electricity reached Bumbuna Town and Kamankay in 2014 after local protests and a direct appeal to the president, that it is expensive and reaches only a handful of wealthier households, that there is almost no electricity in Kamathor and none in the chiefdom's other 42 villages.

The claim that Kadala and Kamathor were left out of compensation is from one independent source, a 2024 master's thesis based on field interviews, and the Bank's documents do not mention those two villages. Note that this map already carries a separate case at the same place, 'Tonkolili Iron Ore and the Bumbuna Shootings', which concerns African Minerals' iron ore operation and a police shooting in Bumbuna town in April 2012. That is a different operation with a different financier; the two are not one episode.

lvwhy.project: An IDA grant financed the environmental and social management of the dam, including the resettlement plans for the reservoir and the transmission line.
lvwhy.land: Farmland and houses were taken for the reservoir, a buffer zone, a conservation area and the transmission line right of way.

cases.title: Ribb dam and Megech irrigation: 227 households moved to towns, 6,618 people unpaid at closing
cases.place: Ribb dam and reservoir, Farta and Ebinat woredas, South Gondar, Amhara, Ethiopia
cases.point: Debre Tabor, one of the two towns the displaced households were moved to (OpenStreetMap). The Bank's documents give no coordinates for the dam or the reservoir.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-43330 and IDA-49760 for the Ethiopia Irrigation and Drainage Project, also called the Ethiopian Nile Irrigation and Drainage Project (P092353). US$100 million approved 21 June 2007, effective 24 January 2008, with US$60 million of additional financing approved 23 June 2011 (P125307). The original total of US$160 million was revised to US$121.3 million and US$105.8 million was disbursed. Closing was extended from 31 October 2015 to 31 October 2017. The project was environmental category A. The implementing agency was the Ministry of Water, Irrigation and Electricity. Bank performance was rated Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 10 January 2019).

cases.conditions: The project triggered the involuntary resettlement policy and four environmental policies, including safety of dams. Seven resettlement action plans were approved by the Bank, three for Megech-Seraba, one for Ribb and three for the Ribb dam, with compensation and livelihood restoration costed at US$21.7 million. The Bank's policy required compensation before works began. In October 2017, the final restructuring changed the financing plan so that credit money could pay cash compensation to 6,618 affected people and livelihood restoration payments to 1,486 of them, US$9.68 million in total, after the credit had closed.
cases.community: The dam at Ribb and the irrigation schemes at Megech-Seraba and Ribb took farmland in the Lake Tana basin. The Bank's completion report says that by the end of the project 6,618 project-affected persons had been identified and still needed to be paid, either for temporary loss of access to land during redistribution and construction or for permanent relocation because of the Ribb dam and reservoir, which the government financed. Its table of compensation payments gives 3,210 eligible people at Megech-Seraba, 3,180 at Ribb irrigation and drainage, and 226 at the Ribb dam and reservoir. The report says the government funded only US$11.17 million of the US$21.7 million the plans had costed. A 2020 master's thesis at Addis Ababa University by Teketel Adefres, which surveyed 115 of the households, gives a different and more specific count from an Ethiopian Ministry of Water, Irrigation and Energy livelihood relocation report of 2018: 1,486 households on the final net list of affected households, of whom 227 lost all their farmland and housing and were moved to the towns of Ebinat and Debre Tabor, where they were given urban plots for houses and working areas for licensed groups. The affected kebeles it names are Medeb Gubda, Jara Shekera and Ayva Niva in Farta woreda and Ziha and Amisteya in Ibinat woreda. The thesis finds that 6.96 per cent of the affected households had access to all basic services, that 8.7 per cent had received income-generating activities and that 33.0 per cent had market access.
cases.displaced_label: households that lost all farmland and housing and were moved to Ebinat and Debre Tabor towns (Ethiopian Ministry of Water, Irrigation and Energy relocation report of 2018, as given in Adefres, 2020)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 10,409 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives 6,618 project-affected persons identified and unpaid at the end of the project, covering both temporary loss of access to land and permanent relocation, and a table listing 226 eligible people at the Ribb dam and reservoir, 3,210 at Megech-Seraba and 3,180 at Ribb irrigation. The 2020 thesis, citing the Ethiopian ministry's 2018 relocation report, gives 1,486 affected households of whom 227 were relocated. The Bank's figure of 1,486 is given as persons and the ministry's as households. The documents do not explain these differences and no document found reconciles them with ICIJ's figure.
cases.outcome: The Bank rated social safeguards performance unsatisfactory, 'primarily due to protracted delays in making compensation payments and supporting livelihood restoration for the PAPs in the Ribb reservoir and dam construction site'. It says the delays caused 'increasing frustration on the part of the affected communities and rising tension in the project areas', that communities had little incentive to give up their land and to some extent damaged installed infrastructure, and that 'throughout much of the project implementation period, the project was not in compliance with OP 4.12 and posed high social risk. It was only after credit closure that the project could be brought into compliance through the use of the Credit to cover the costs.' Its review of Bank performance says the outstanding issues at the end of the project posed flood risks, dam safety risks and reputational risk tied to the 6,616 people who 'were not compensated, lost their livelihoods, lost access to utility services, or were at risk of being encircled by the Ribb reservoir'. Of the 4,000 hectares targeted at Megech-Seraba only 1,000 hectares were ready for use, and the Bank's economic analysis at closing found the project not economically viable. Bank management refused a further extension. The 2020 thesis concludes that the livelihoods of the resettled households are largely unsustainable.

cases.title: Kibera and Mukuru railway relocation: 1,256 households moved, the rest left waiting
cases.place: Kibera and Mukuru settlements along the Kenya-Uganda railway, Nairobi, Kenya
cases.point: Kibera, Nairobi (OpenStreetMap), at one of the two three-kilometre safety zones. The second is in Mukuru, about 11 km east.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-4147 (SDR 18.2 million, US$25.6 million), IDA-4148 (SDR 83.03 million, US$117.3 million), IDA-4149 (SDR 25.5 million, US$35.9 million), grant IDA-H2020 (SDR 10.4 million, US$14.6 million) and additional credit IDA-4977 (SDR 18.6 million, US$26.2 million) for the East Africa Trade and Transport Facilitation Project (P079734), covering Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania. Approved 24 January 2006, effective 5 June 2006, closing extended from 30 September 2011 to 30 September 2015. Additional financing of US$30 million was approved in June 2011 for the enlarged relocation plan, and the project's safeguards category was changed from B to A at the same time. Actual IDA financing was US$225.51 million. The line item for implementing the relocation action plan rose from US$11.00 million at appraisal to US$92.80 million actual, of which IDA paid US$39.10 million and the government of Kenya US$53.70 million. Outcome was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 September 2016; Independent Evaluation Group ICR Review, 9 May 2017).

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA partial risk guarantees)
lenders.role: Guarantee IDA-B0090 of up to US$45 million for the Kenyan subsidiary and IDA-B0100 of up to US$15 million for the Ugandan subsidiary of Rift Valley Railways Holdings Limited, the concessionaire of the Kenya-Uganda railway (World Bank completion report).

cases.conditions: The project funded a relocation action plan to clear a safety zone along the railway through two informal settlements. The Bank wanted the cleared strip kept to 10.4 metres, 5.2 metres each side of the tracks; the government of Kenya wanted 60 metres. After a train derailment in Kibera in 2009 the government returned to the wider figure, and a new plan in January 2011 set a right of way of 40 metres with resettlement of households in the next 10 metres on each side, a total work area of 60 metres in two three-kilometre safety zones, one in Kibera and one in Mukuru, with a nine-metre wall between the settlements and the tracks. A Resettlement Management Unit was set up in 2011. When it became clear the plan could not be finished by closing, the government agreed to put about US$860,000 from the remaining credit into an escrow account for owners of multiple plots.

companies.name: Rift Valley Railways Holdings Limited
companies.role: Concessionaire of the Kenya-Uganda railway, whose Kenyan and Ugandan subsidiaries held the IDA partial risk guarantees
companies.desc: Holding company of the 25-year concession to run the Kenya-Uganda railway. The World Bank's completion report records the weak performance of the concession as a serious shortfall of the project's early years.

cases.community: The Bank's completion report says the expropriation was first estimated at 3,400 structures or households, 'involving possibly 10,000 people', in settlements it puts at about 250,000 residents for Mukuru and about 1 million for Kibera, and that after the 2011 plan 'the number of households requiring resettlement grew from 3,400 to about 10,000, involving some 30,000 people'. By the end of January 2016, 51 per cent of the needed residential units and 29 per cent of the needed business units had been built and 1,256 households had been relocated. By September 2016 a social audit had cut the requirement from 9,005 units to 7,429 and 3,214 affected people had been relocated; 324 pupils had moved from informal schools to ten public schools; 70 grievance cases were pending before the Grievance Appeals Board. The Independent Evaluation Group puts the 1,256 households and 3,214 people at just over 13 per cent and 10 per cent of the estimated totals, and says the relocation programme was only 30 per cent complete at closing and still going on in January 2017. Amnesty International, in an urgent action of 15 April 2010, recorded that Kenya Railways had placed notices in newspapers on 21 March telling people living and working in shacks by the lines that they would be prosecuted unless they tore down their shacks and left within 30 days, and that more than 50,000 people were at risk of forced eviction with no alternative housing or resettlement offered. It noted that a Relocation Action Plan for Improving Safety along the Kenya Railway Line, commissioned after similar eviction plans in 2005, had never been implemented.
cases.killed_note: A train derailment in Kibera in 2009 caused several fatalities, according to the Bank's completion report, which gives no number. Those deaths are not counted here: the derailment was a railway accident, not an act of the project, and the report ties it to the project only in that it let the government press for a wider cleared strip.
cases.displaced_label: households relocated by the end of January 2016 (World Bank completion report; Independent Evaluation Group)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 11,722 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives 1,256 households relocated by the end of January 2016 and 3,214 project-affected persons relocated by September 2016, and says the plan after 2011 covered about 10,000 households and some 30,000 people. The Independent Evaluation Group calls the relocated numbers just over 13 per cent and 10 per cent of the estimated totals and the programme 30 per cent complete at closing. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Independent Evaluation Group rated the project's outcome moderately unsatisfactory and said the relocation plan, revised in 2011, only started in late 2013 and was incomplete at closing. The Bank's own lesson from the project is that it treated the clearance 'as a standard linear resettlement typically associated with a road or rail investment', that this is hard to apply in settlements like Kibera and Mukuru, that the government 'clearly wanted to clear the whole reserve', and that the work 'goes well beyond compliance with OP 4.12'. Residents of Soweto, Laini Saba and Mashimoni who gave up their homes for promised flats at Ng'ando in Jamhuri Estate told the Daily Nation they were still in temporary structures without latrines or running water; the article says 560 families petitioned Parliament to make Kenya Railways resettle them, that the plan had called for 9,005 units between 2013 and 2015, and that of more than 600 units in their scheme about 100 were complete except for the sewer line, about 300 were unfinished and deteriorating and about 200 had not been started. Kenya Railways told the paper it had not received government funds to finish the work; residents said it still sent rent reminders for the unfinished units.

cases.title: Kawanda-Masaka power line: armed police used to string a line over unpaid land
cases.place: Kawanda-Masaka 220 kV transmission line corridor, from Wakiso to Masaka, Uganda
cases.point: Nyendo, Masaka City (OpenStreetMap), at the southern end of the 137 km line. The Bank's documents give no coordinates for Galatiya or for the villages named in the resettlement plan.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49880 (IDA Credit No. 4988-UG) for the Uganda Electricity Sector Development Project (P119737). US$120 million approved 30 June 2011, effective 23 October 2012, revised to US$76.04 million, US$60.56 million disbursed, against a borrower contribution of US$33.2 million of which US$18.6 million was spent. Closing was extended from 28 February 2017 to 31 January 2019. Funds were cancelled at a third restructuring on 18 July 2018. Outcome was rated Moderately Satisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 February 2021).

cases.conditions: A resettlement action plan for the 137 km line was disclosed in Uganda on 13 December 2010. The Bank's resettlement policy required compensation before any civil works began. The government set up an escrow account to fund compensation payments. The implementing agency was the Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited (UETCL).

companies.name: Uganda Electricity Transmission Company Limited (UETCL)
companies.role: State transmission company; implementing agency for the line and for the resettlement plan
companies.desc: Uganda's state-owned electricity transmission company, which owns and operates the high-voltage grid and acts as single buyer of bulk power.

cases.community: The project's resettlement plan, reviewed and updated in June 2011, counted 2,136 households and 'about 13596 persons affected by the currently optimized route in the project area', of whom 160 households were to be physically displaced and had chosen to have their houses replaced, while 65 more households with structures to be demolished chose cash. It listed 321 permanent and 121 semi-permanent structures affected and about 225 structures, mainly homes and shops, to be demolished, and named Nabusanke Town A, Kayabwe, Buwama B, Lutente, Lukuli, Kayirikiti, Kalagala Kiteredde, Kamungomba and Namansenene among the places where most of the people to be physically displaced lived, along with the urban centres of Buwama, Lukaaya and Masaka Town Council. The Bank's completion report says the line as built affected 2,661 households against the estimate of 2,136, that 13,642 resettlement packages were prepared, that 89 per cent of affected people had been paid at closing on 31 January 2019 and 93 per cent by December 2020. It records a case at Galatiya where a church sold its land, including a right of way UETCL had already paid for, to squatters; the Bank received three written complaints between May 2017 and February 2018 that UETCL had gone ahead with construction without compensating them, and 'UETCL acquired an interim court order and with the aid of armed policemen forcefully carried out works in the disputed area, which contravened OP/BP 4.12'. After a Bank mission in April 2018 the Bank wrote to UETCL asking it not to enforce the order, not to evict the title holders and not to complete works before compensation; 'UETCL went ahead and carried out the stringing works in contravention of the World Bank safeguards policy, and the landowners commenced legal proceedings against UETCL.' Residents of Nyendo-Ssenyange Division in Masaka told the Daily Monitor they had not been fully paid for their property and land, that a promised disturbance allowance had never come and that their money had not been processed since 2008; a UETCL compensation officer told the paper the project never provided for disturbance allowances. The article's text is dated 29 June 2015 and its page metadata 19 January 2021.
cases.ecosystem: The line passed through the fringes of seven central forest reserves and one local forest reserve, affecting 32.07 hectares in the corridor. As an offset, 210 hectares were restored in the degraded Gangu central forest reserve in Mpigi and Butambala districts and 10 hectares in Nabijoka local forest reserve in Kalungu district. The Bank also records that the project did not comply with Uganda's wetlands regulations because the conditions on its licence, including culverts to let water flow through wetlands, had not been met.
cases.suppression: UETCL used an interim court order and armed police to carry out works in the disputed area at Galatiya while the occupants were unpaid, which the Bank's completion report says contravened its involuntary resettlement policy.
cases.displaced_label: households affected by the line as built (World Bank completion report); the resettlement plan had set 160 households for physical displacement
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 13,596 for this project. That figure appears word for word in the project's own 2011 resettlement plan, which says there are 'in general 2136 households, and a total of about 13596 persons affected by the currently optimized route'. It is a count of people affected, not relocated: the same plan says 160 of those households were to be physically displaced. The Bank's completion report says the line as built affected 2,661 households and that 13,642 resettlement packages were prepared, and records that the line was de-energized in July 2018 'to allow for safe relocation of all households living within the line's ROW corridor', without giving a number for how many were moved.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report says that because of unresolved disputes with landowners and delays in transferring land titles, 'construction works continued along the transmission line, which contravened OP/BP 4.12', and that the slow resolution of the disputes led to conflicts, some reported directly to the Bank. UETCL energized the line on 1 June 2018 without telling the Bank 'and without considering the PAPs and business operators who were still under the line'; the Bank intervened and the line was de-energized on 23 July 2018 to allow households inside the corridor to be moved and the safety issues dealt with, and was re-energized on 19 December 2018. The report says the resettlement plan's implementation was also marred by governance issues that led to the dismissal of the project safeguards officer, and that the only compliance issue still open was the outstanding payments, at 93 per cent of affected people paid. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 29 June 2021 records the same events and lists lengthy delays in processing payment claims among the problems.

cases.title: Upper Cisokan pumped storage: 765 households moved, a decade of unfinished payments
cases.place: Upper Cisokan reservoirs, access road and quarry, Cipongkor and Rongga districts, West Bandung Regency, West Java, Indonesia
cases.point: Cipongkor district, West Bandung Regency (OpenStreetMap), where the project's quarry and part of its access road sit. The reservoirs also reach Rongga district and the Cibeber and Bojongpicung districts of Cianjur Regency.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-80570 for the Upper Cisokan Pumped Storage Hydro-Electrical Power (1040 MW) Project (P112158), later renamed the Pumped Storage Technical Assistance Project. US$640 million approved 26 May 2011, effective 1 May 2012, revised to US$36.09 million after the project was restructured on 21 December 2018, with US$36.09 million disbursed. Closing was extended from 31 December 2018 to 31 December 2021. The borrower's share was US$160 million at approval and US$77.91 million spent. Total project cost fell from US$800 million to US$114 million (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 June 2022).

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD), successor loan
lenders.role: The Bank re-engaged with the scheme through the Development of Pumped Storage Hydropower in Java Bali System Project (P172256, approved 10 September 2021). The Bank's completion report says it was agreed that an action plan on the outstanding land acquisition and resettlement issues, acceptable to the Bank, be fulfilled before that new loan disburses for Upper Cisokan.

cases.conditions: The loan agreement said the borrower must ensure that component 2 of the project, land acquisition, resettlement and rehabilitation, 'is financed exclusively out of its own or other resources and not out' of the Bank loan. The state utility PLN undertook to finance US$160 million for that component, including US$74.4 million of land acquisition. Three land acquisition and resettlement action plans were prepared under the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, for the upper and lower reservoirs, for the access road and quarry, and for the transmission lines; the Bank cleared them in 2011 and kept monitoring them after the 2018 restructuring. The Bank's own completion report notes that the US$74.4 million estimate for land acquisition and compensation was not included in a cost figure it gives elsewhere.

companies.name: PT PLN (Perusahaan Listrik Negara)
companies.role: State electricity utility; borrower's implementing agency, which financed and carried out the land acquisition and resettlement
companies.desc: Indonesia's state-owned electricity company, which generates, transmits and distributes most of the country's power.

cases.community: The Bank's completion report says in a footnote that 'the number of households affected by land acquisition was 2,063, including 765 households who were physically resettled'. It says delays in land acquisition and resettlement were flagged as a key risk at the start and that the risk materialised: 'it took a full decade for the acquisition and resettlement to be substantially completed', including compensation payments and livelihood assistance. A review of the resettlement plans that the Bank approved in May 2021 found outstanding items: all remaining land compensation payments to be delivered, compensation for restricting land use inside the transmission line right of way to be delivered, infrastructure support for eligible communities, and 'complete relocation of remaining households in the Upper and Lower Cisokan Reservoirs'. A separate count in the same report says that as of February 2021 the project had acquired 721.92 hectares, 98.65 per cent of the total. The project's land acquisition plan for the access road and quarry names Karangsari village in Cipongkor district as the quarry site and runs the access road through Cijambu, Sarinagen, Sirnagalih, Sukaresmi and Cibitung villages in Cipongkor and Rongga districts. Republika reported on 18 November 2015 that a lawyer for residents, Roedy Wiranatakusumah, accused PLN of building an access road on a 5,130 square metre plot in Sukaresmi village, Rongga district, while a court case over it was still running; the plot's certificate holder, Sulton, said he had never sold the land. iNews reported on 21 June 2025 that at least 24 houses in Karangsari village, Cipongkor, had cracked walls from rock blasting and crushing at PLN's Gunung Karang andesite quarry for the scheme, that residents of neighbouring Sarinagen also protested, that PLN had offered a one-off payment of 200,000 rupiah which residents had not accepted, and that a West Bandung council commission chairman, Pither Tjuandys, called the amount far too small for a state company. PLN's regional manager, Nugroho Budi Sulaksono, told the paper the houses would be repaired in about a week and that most of the damage was minor.
cases.displaced_label: households physically resettled (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 8,213 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives 2,063 households affected by land acquisition, of which 765 households were physically resettled, and says relocation of the remaining households in the two reservoir areas was still outstanding when the Bank reviewed the plans in May 2021. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Bank's loan was cut from US$640 million to US$36.09 million and the project was renamed a technical assistance project in December 2018; the dam itself was not built under this loan. Compensation payment for household resettlement was recorded as completed in July 2019, eight years after the loan was approved and after the original closing date. The Bank's own review of the resettlement plans in May 2021 still listed outstanding land compensation payments, outstanding payment for restrictions inside the transmission line corridor and the relocation of households still living in the reservoir areas, and made an acceptable action plan on these a condition of disbursement under the successor loan. PLN's own completion review of the plans, finished in 2021, identified outstanding tasks and new issues that had emerged.

cases.title: Kenya's informal settlements upgrading project: six deaths the Bank was not told about
cases.place: Majengo Talai in Kericho and Kwa Hakatsa and Mwatate in Mombasa, among KISIP settlements in 14 Kenyan counties
cases.point: Kericho town (OpenStreetMap), where one of the three settlements needing relocation to other land lies. The project worked in settlements across 14 counties and the Bank's documents give no coordinates.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-48730 and trust fund TF-18327 for the Kenya Informal Settlements Improvement Project (P113542). US$100 million of IDA approved 24 March 2011, effective 30 June 2011, with US$99.99 million disbursed by the revised figures and US$93.29 million actually disbursed; the trust fund added US$8.3 million. Closing was extended twice, from 30 June 2016 to 31 May 2018 and then to 30 November 2019. Outcome was rated Satisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 14 August 2020).

lenders.role: US$45 million at appraisal, revised to US$39 million, with US$38.95 million disbursed (World Bank completion report).

lenders.name: Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sweden)
lenders.role: US$10 million at appraisal, revised to US$8.3 million and fully disbursed through trust fund TF-18327 (World Bank completion report).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered three policies: environmental assessment, cultural property and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework was disclosed on 26 November 2010 and re-disclosed after the mid-term review. Settlement-level resettlement action plans were required where planning, surveying or infrastructure work displaced people; about 70 were needed for the tenure component. The Bank also required that land titles not be released until land for the affected people had been identified and surveyed.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report says the infrastructure component had about 30,000 project-affected persons, roughly 2 per cent of its beneficiaries, and the tenure component about 18,000, roughly 14 per cent. It says all displacement was in-situ, inside the settlement, 'except for three settlements in Kericho and Mombasa (Kwa Hakatsa, Mwatate and Majengo Talai) where alternative land was required to resettle 82 households (328 PAPs) as they were living on environmentally fragile areas and could not be settled in-situ'. At project closing that move had not happened: land had been identified in Mombasa and the planning and resettlement process had begun, and two options for land were still being explored in Kericho. Of about 70 resettlement plans needed where tenure work caused displacement, 61 had been cleared and about 40 had been implemented or nearly implemented when the completion report was written. The grievance system handled complaints at settlement, county and national level. Separately, the report records six deaths: during an October 2018 mission, after the Bank asked the client to confirm all incidents involving the project's works or vehicles, 'the Bank team learned that six fatalities had occurred'. It says the first sign came from a review of a monthly progress report, and that although there was awareness at local level to report severe injuries and deaths to resident engineers, contractors and the police, 'there was a systemic failure of reporting to KISIP high level management and to the World Bank'.
cases.ecosystem: At project closing many of the drainage networks the project built were clogged with solid waste and wastewater, because residents and counties had not worked out how to collect waste and maintain the upgraded infrastructure.
cases.killed_note: Six deaths in incidents involving the project's works or vehicles, in 2015 and 2018, recorded in the World Bank's completion report. At the time the report was written one case was treated as resolved, three were in court, one was with an insurance company and one was still in discussion with the contractor; the Bank says the project team committed to enforcing the contracts until the affected families were compensated, with a deadline of the end of August 2020.
cases.displaced_label: households (328 people) required to move to other land, not yet moved at project closing (World Bank completion report)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 7,952 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives about 30,000 project-affected persons under the infrastructure component and about 18,000 under the tenure component, says all displacement was in-situ apart from 82 households (328 people) in three settlements who needed other land, and records that their resettlement had not been completed when the project closed. No document found counts people actually relocated. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome satisfactory. At closing five of the six death cases were unresolved and the Bank said its supervision would continue until they were, and that the resettlement of the 82 households and the remaining resettlement plans, expected to be finished in September 2020, would also be supervised past closing. An action plan including a protocol for reporting incidents was put in place after the fatalities came to light.

cases.title: Lower Nzoia irrigation: 568 people unpaid at closing and two drownings
cases.place: Lower Nzoia irrigation scheme and flood dykes, Busia and Siaya counties, Kenya
cases.point: Budalang'i, Bunyala, Busia County (OpenStreetMap), inside the scheme's flood protection and irrigation area. The project also covered Siaya County and a water distribution network in Mombasa.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-52680 (US$155 million), IDA-56740 (US$58 million) and IDA-74230 (US$30 million) and trust fund TF-A0761 (US$3.5 million) for the Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635). Approved 18 June 2013, effective 24 October 2013, closed 31 May 2025. Bank financing of US$243 million was revised down to US$141.24 million with US$147.32 million disbursed. Credits were partly cancelled at restructurings on 4 September 2017 and 25 June 2019 and the closing date was extended four times (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 December 2025).

lenders.name: KfW (Germany)
lenders.role: US$20.01 million in the original financing plan, revised to nil, with US$14,985 recorded as disbursed (World Bank completion report).

cases.conditions: The project triggered the Bank's involuntary resettlement and environmental assessment policies, along with pest management and physical cultural resources. Four resettlement action plans were prepared by the borrower and cleared by the Bank, for the Lower Nzoia irrigation scheme, the flood infrastructure and the Mombasa water distribution network. The project was restructured to allow land compensation to be paid from IDA funds through a special-purpose account separate from the government's pooled land compensation account, which meant a National Land Commission bank account had to be opened for the purpose.
cases.community: The Bank's completion report says that at project closure, 'of the 4,704 PAPs, 88 percent were compensated, while the remaining were 568 PAPs (12 percent) with a value of around US$883,000', and attributes the shortfall to absentee claimants, succession grants, pending affidavits and missing title documents. It says the borrower remains liable and that the National Land Commission must ringfence the money until the unpayable claimants become eligible. It also records 156 grievances about compensation, safeguards, construction and access, of which 142 were resolved; of the 14 left, 11 were about pending compensation. The report describes land valuation and payment processing as slow, with payment processing alone taking three to four months on average, and says insufficient government funding for compensation added to the delays. It says it was initially unclear which farmers were affected or how they would be paid, and that the lack of specific funding for crop compensation caused delays. The Star reported on 8 November 2022 that residents of Ugunja, Alego Usonga and Ugenya sub-counties in Siaya and Budalang'i in Busia accepted the project but objected to the 7-metre-wide tertiary canals, which would leave smallholders with little or no land, feared the government would not pay for the land taken for them, and wanted to know where they would be relocated; it says compensation for the main and secondary canals had largely been settled from Ugunja to Block 7 in Usonga ward while the tertiary canals remained unresolved, and that the National Land Commission's compensation gazette notice was dated 21 June 2021.
cases.killed_note: Two deaths by drowning during the project's construction period, recorded in the World Bank's completion report, which says all construction was immediately suspended, an investigation into the causes was carried out and corrective actions were taken.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 9,079 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives 4,704 project-affected persons, of whom 88 per cent were compensated and 568 were not, with no breakdown between people who lost land and people who lost homes and no count of anyone relocated. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 15 May 2026 repeats the same figures. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
cases.outcome: The Bank's rating for involuntary resettlement was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory by 2018. At closing 568 claimants worth about US$883,000 were still unpaid, and the Bank said it would monitor the post-closure safeguard action plan twice a year, including through the follow-on project. Of the irrigation works, supporting structures for a second phase were built but the Bank's completion report records that land compensation and related social and environmental problems delayed handing sites to the contractor.

cases.title: Ethiopia's third road sector loan: over 30 deaths and no count of the people displaced
cases.place: Gondar-Debark, Aposto-Bore-Negele, Gedo-Nekempte and Yalo-Nehile roads, Ethiopia
cases.point: Gondar (OpenStreetMap), at one end of the Gondar-Debark road, one of the four corridors. The Bank's documents do not say where the deaths happened.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-43150 and trust fund TF-56516 for the Road Sector Development Program Support Project III, an adaptable programme loan (P091077). SDR 148.7 million, equivalent to US$225 million, approved 31 May 2007, effective 21 August 2007, mid-term review 21 November 2011, closed 30 June 2015. The implementing agency was the Ethiopian Roads Authority. One component, institutional strengthening of the roads authority, was dropped at a restructuring in 2013 (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 December 2015).

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A, full assessment, and triggered the environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement policies. Environmental impact assessments and resettlement action plans were prepared for each of the project roads, together with a resettlement and rehabilitation policy framework. Contractors were bound by environmental monitoring plans, with internal monitoring by the roads authority's environmental monitoring and safety branch and external monitoring by regional and national environmental authorities.
cases.community: The loan upgraded or rehabilitated the Gondar-Debark trunk road, the 268 km Aposto-Bore-Negele link road and the 134 km Gedo-Nekempte section of the Addis-Nekempte road, and built the 70 km Yalo-Nehile regional gravel road. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the number of project-affected persons was estimated at appraisal at 3,477 households and 19,877 persons, with resettlement costed at US$285.5 million, and that 'the ICR does not provide any information on the actual number of persons affected by the project' and 'there is no evidence in the ICR that this category A project complied with the involuntary safeguard requirements'. The Bank's completion report says its own finding is that 'the overall performance of the project on safeguards aspects was very weak with relatively very few gains achieved for enhancing the management of social and environmental concerns', that early supervision reports describe deplorable working conditions, in at least one case reported to local authorities and perhaps the cause of worker strikes, and that there is room for improvement in carrying out land acquisition, resettlement and compensation and in the pay and conditions of workers. It says the roads authority's capacity on safeguards was weak, that the regions and districts that actually carry out land acquisition and expropriation 'have little knowledge or awareness of the project's safeguards instruments', and that the roads authority's right-of-way team is not resourced to monitor the resettlement plans. The last outstanding items on one contract included 'resolution of the outstanding ROW compensation issues for the extended contract period'.
cases.ecosystem: The Bank's completion report records deficiencies in environmental mitigation during construction: treatment of cut slopes, reinstatement of quarry sites and borrow pits, disposal of spoil material and handling of bitumen and oils.
cases.killed_note: Footnote 10 of the World Bank's completion report says 'over 30 deaths were reported in several incidents due road crashes and improper safety procedures with use of heavy equipment'. The Independent Evaluation Group repeats the figure and attributes the deaths to contractors not complying with basic road safety requirements and to the roads authority not having the staff to supervise them. The report says the dead were construction workers, road users and community residents. The figure of 30 is used here because the documents give no exact number.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 15,015 for this project. The Bank's appraisal estimate, as recorded by the Independent Evaluation Group, was 3,477 households and 19,877 persons affected. The Independent Evaluation Group says the completion report gives no information on the actual number of people affected, and no document found counts anyone relocated. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at. No displacement figure is given here because none of the Bank's documents records an outcome.
cases.outcome: The Bank's completion report rated safeguards performance very weak and said health and safety concerns led to 'the unnecessary and preventable loss of lives and properties in the project contracts'. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 November 2016 says there is no explicit statement in the completion report about compliance with environmental safeguards and no evidence that this category A project complied with the involuntary resettlement requirements. The Bank says the roads authority's commitment and capacity improved in later years, across its whole portfolio and not only on Bank-financed projects.

Neither document names the places where the deaths happened, gives an exact number, or counts anyone relocated, and the Independent Evaluation Group says the completion report gives no information on the actual number of people affected. Those are different corridors and different loans.

extend.why: Lead 8 is the same loan as this case: the Uganda Transport Sector Development Project, P092837. The existing card covers the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road. The project's completion report adds documented compensation shortfalls on two other corridors under the same credits that are not on the card, and firmer figures for the loan itself.

lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA), full credit detail
lenders_add.role: Credit IDA-46790, SDR 120 million (US$190 million equivalent), approved 10 December 2009; additional credit IDA-49490, SDR 47.4 million (US$75 million equivalent); and grant TF-11094 of GBP 6.05 million (US$8.0 million equivalent) for the Transport Sector Development Project (P092837). The Bank suspended disbursements and then cancelled the credits on 21 December 2015, with the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road 49 per cent complete; the government continued the road with its own funds (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 5 June 2017).

add.community_add: The same credits also paid for two roads in northern Uganda, and the completion report gives compensation shortfalls on both. On the Gulu-Atiak road, 1,884 of 2,027 affected people were compensated, 93 per cent, with ten of the unpaid claims in court and the rest awaiting reassessment. On the Vurra-Oraba road, 3,276 of 3,935 were compensated, 83 per cent; the report says the shortfall arose because extra affected people were identified after compensation was supposed to have been concluded and no money had been budgeted for land acquisition that year, and records over 200 complaints of non-payment from bounced payments and missing documents. On the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road itself the report says 2,246 of 2,844 identified people had been compensated, 79 per cent, rising to 94 per cent by 27 March 2017, and that the original estimate of 2,430 was based on a sample rather than a full census, with another 414 people added later by surveyors and valuers. It says road construction started and continued before most affected people were paid.
add.conditions_add: The 2011 environmental and social impact assessment for the Kamwenge-Fort Portal road proposed category A; during preparation of the additional financing this was downgraded to category B. The Bank's completion report calls that change 'an error of judgment', given the social problems that emerged and the fact that 13.3 km of the road runs through Kibale National Park. On 22 December 2014 the Uganda Wildlife Authority approved the wider road cross-section through the park, an option the impact assessment had rejected, on condition that only a limited number of trees be removed and extra speed humps installed.
add.displaced_note_add: ICIJ gives 12,882 for this project. The Bank's completion report counts people identified for compensation rather than people relocated: 2,027 on Gulu-Atiak, 3,935 on Vurra-Oraba and 2,844 on Kamwenge-Fort Portal. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.

extend.why: Lead 27, Madagascar's Integrated Growth Poles project (P083351), is the World Bank operation the existing card already names through MIGA's guarantee. lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA), Integrated Growth Poles Project
lenders_add.role: The Integrated Growth Poles Project (P083351) was approved on 12 July 2005 and closed on 31 December 2014, with additional financing (P110405) approved on 17 April 2008. The project covered Antananarivo-Antsirabe, Nosy Be and Taolagnaro (Fort Dauphin). Its Fort Dauphin component built a new public port on the Ehoala peninsula under a public-private partnership with Rio Tinto and part-rehabilitated the existing port. The Bank's completion report lists, among the component's safeguards activities, 'implementation of RAPs for the QMM's mining facility and Ehoala Port' and water supply and sanitation schemes for project-affected people. Because the Bank financed Ehoala Port as an associated investment supporting Rio Tinto's mining, Rio Tinto also had to comply with Bank safeguard policies. The project was environmental category A and an independent expert advisory panel monitored safeguards compliance (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 15 June 2015).

add.community_add: The Bank's completion report says QMM's mining investment 'created significant safeguards challenges in the mining communes', that the income and livelihood restoration programme QMM ran for residents of the mining communes 'was marked by recurring disputes over the prices the company paid to buy their land and the employment policy at its mining facility', and that this led residents at various times to blockade QMM construction sites and facilities, 'with the most recent flare up in early 2013 when they blocked the mine compound entrance, trapping more than 200 staff inside'. It says grievance mechanisms set up by the Bank and QMM's social programmes helped manage the disputes and prevent violent escalation but that tensions linger among residents 'who still feel they were unfairly compensated'. A table in the report's annex, sourced to Rio Tinto's own 2009 information report, lists 'support to the populations affected by the resettlement scheme' through monetary compensation, restitution in kind, house rehabilitation and support measures, naming the resettled population, affected people at Ilafitsinana and villagers from Lohalovoka and Ambinanibe, with the World Bank among the parties involved; it also lists compensation to fishermen and to the people of Ambinanibe, Lohalovoka and Ilafitsinana. The report also records an acute bout of consumer price inflation during construction of the mine and the port.
add.displaced_note_add: ICIJ gives 8,911 displaced for Madagascar's Integrated Growth Poles project, drawn from World Bank documents and current to 31 December 2014. The Bank's completion report for that project names the resettlement plans and the villages involved but gives no count of households or people relocated, and the figures in its annex come from Rio Tinto's own report rather than from the Bank. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
